S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
examples: Raises hand or blurts out the answer before the question is even finished in class or meetings.
Jumps to conclusions and speaks before the other person finishes their sentence.
Answers hastily without reading the question to the end in quizzes or exams.
Interrupts and answers in the middle of a conversation without listening to the other person until the end.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized chiefly by excessive motor activity, difficulty inhibiting impulses, and poor regulation of activity level relative to context, with inattention often present but less prominent than hyperactivity and impulsivity. Clinically, patients may show a long-standing pattern of being "on the go," acting before thinking, interrupting others, and struggling to wait, which leads to functional impairment at school, work, or in relationships. The disorder typically has onset in childhood, but may not be formally recognized until later when environmental demands for sustained self-control, planning, and behavioral restraint increase. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasiveness across settings, and the absence of discrete episodes or primary mood-driven or situationally bound impulsive behavior.

patient.personality: Jonathan is an outgoing, competitively driven and impulsive young entrepreneur who thrives on new tech ideas and social energy but tends to work in a laid-back, chaotic, last-minute style.
patient.stressor: Just over two years ago, during the final stretch of his accelerated bachelor’s program, Jonathan began trying to juggle full-time coursework with launching multiple online business ventures and maintaining a highly active social and gaming life. The escalating academic demands for sustained, stepwise work—long projects, group assignments with clear role expectations, and detailed instructions—collided with his preference for improvisation and rapid shifts between interests. Over the ensuing semesters, he repeatedly committed to ambitious projects and internships but struggled to carry out the structured parts of them, leading to incomplete coursework, frustrated teammates, and the collapse of a few promising e-commerce ideas, which undermined both his grades and his confidence in his entrepreneurial potential. After graduating but failing to follow through on several early-stage startup opportunities and feeling mounting pressure from family about his lack of stable progress, he sought psychiatric care at the suggestion of a mentor who suspected that his long-standing difficulty sticking with instructions and finishing tasks might reflect an underlying attentional and impulse-control issue rather than mere laziness.
patient.chief_complaint: “I start things fine, but I just can’t seem to follow through on instructions and finish what I’m supposed to do.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: If I’m watching a lecture video or trying to go through a long spec sheet for one of my startups, I’ll stay locked in for maybe five minutes and then my brain just drifts off to Discord, random business ideas, or what game I want to play next, and I realize I’ve missed whole chunks without even noticing it happen.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: I’ll get super hyped about a new class project or startup idea, map out the first steps, and then just stall halfway through the boring, detailed parts—like filling out forms, finishing reports, or actually submitting assignments—so I end up with a trail of half-built websites, half-written essays, and missed deadlines that I just never circle back to.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: When I look at everything I need to do—assignments, emails, pitch decks, bug fixes—it all feels like one giant messy pile in my head, so I bounce between tasks at random and then suddenly it’s 3 a.m. and nothing important is actually finished even though I’ve been ‘busy’ all day.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: Anytime I’m in a lecture, meeting, or even just on voice chat while we’re gaming, I’m constantly jiggling my leg, spinning a pen, clicking my mouse, or shifting in my chair because sitting still feels almost physically uncomfortable, and people keep telling me it’s distracting.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
S011.manifestation: In long classes or startup meetings I’m supposed to sit through, I keep popping up to refill my water, check something on the whiteboard, or ‘take a quick call,’ but really it’s just that I can’t stand staying in my seat for more than a few minutes at a time.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: It’s like I’ve got this motor running inside me all the time—during movies, family dinners, or even just trying to chill and read something for class, I feel this restless pressure to get up, move around, check my phone, or start doing something else, and I can’t just relax into one thing.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
S016.manifestation: In group discussions or when a mentor is giving me feedback, I’ll jump in with my answer or defense before they’ve even finished their sentence because I already think I know where they’re going, and then I realize I cut them off or totally missed the actual point.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
S017.manifestation: Whether I’m waiting in line at a café, queued up for an in-game match, or sitting outside a professor’s office, I get so impatient that I start checking the time every few seconds, pacing, or trying to skip ahead somehow, because just calmly waiting my turn feels almost unbearable.
